question: Can the printed or spoken content of a mass-produced published work (the text of a book, song lyrics, film dialogue, on-screen subtitles) be recorded as an 'inscription' in the CIDOC CRM / LIDO sense?
gold_answer: No. Both the LIDO Inscriptions element and the CRM's E34 Inscription class are defined as physical lettering or markings affixed to a specific physical carrier, not as the abstract textual content shared by a whole class of mass-produced items. When this was asked about a FRBRoo Manifestation Product Type (which is itself a conceptual, not physical, object), the LIDO co-chair replied that an inscription must be bound to a physical carrier, and that this kind of descriptive or quoted textual content belongs instead in lido:objectDescriptionSet, typed as needed. The exchange also surfaced the questioner's own doubt about whether a conceptual Manifestation Product Type should be described with item-level physical attributes at all, but that side issue was not settled.
key_facts: LIDO's Inscriptions element and the CRM's E34 Inscription are defined as physical lettering/markings affixed to a physical carrier
The LIDO co-chair's answer was that such textual content should go in lido:objectDescriptionSet rather than Inscriptions
The object in question was a FRBRoo Manifestation Product Type, a conceptual (not physical) object, which is why treating it as having a physical inscription was questioned
produced_answer: The archive discusses this directly in thread t0615 (March-April 2012). Michael Hopwood (EDItEUR) asked whether descriptions/transcriptions of text of published books, song lyrics, film/TV dialogue, and words in photos could be recorded as LIDO:Inscriptions, given the object in question is a FRBRoo 'Manifestation Product Type' (a mass-produced conceptual object), not a physical item. Regine Stein answered that an inscription (LIDO's Inscriptions element, aligned with CRM's E34 Inscription) is explicitly bound to a *physical* carrier -- 'physical lettering... affixed, inscribed, or attached to the object/work' -- so this content-description use case does not fit E34/LIDO:Inscriptions; instead it should go into LIDO's objectDescriptionSet, typed as needed. Patrick Le Boeuf offered an alternative FRBRoo-based route for the quoted text itself: model it via F23 Expression Fragment with P3 has note (P3.1 has type E55 Type {quotation}) rather than as an inscription. Hopwood then pushed further, specifically asking to what degree on-screen subtitles in a digital download could be considered an 'inscription' -- but this follow-up question was not answered in the thread; it was left open/unresolved.

question: A book-industry data specialist wanted to map commercial publishing metadata (ONIX) into the museum-oriented LIDO schema. What objections were raised against this, and what range of positions did SIG members take on whether and how it could be done?
gold_answer: Michael Hopwood (representing EDItEUR and the Linked Heritage project) proposed mapping ONIX for Books into LIDO, which required treating a generic manifestation/product as though it were a unique physical item and treating printed text as a kind of 'inscription'; he justified this by the project's mandate to feed book/music/AV data into Europeana. Patrick Le Boeuf objected that the mapping was conceptually impossible, since ONIX describes abstract publications while LIDO is designed for unique physical objects, and argued that stretching 'manifestation as item' or 'text as inscription' was not helpful; he suggested FRBRoo was the correct target instead. Martin Doerr agreed LIDO was not intended for this material and that real interoperability should come from mapping everything to RDF under CRM/FRBRoo rather than repurposing LIDO. Regine Stein took a middle position: she agreed LIDO was not meant to hold this data, but argued the crosswalk exercise was still valuable as an analysis of where LIDO's schema does and doesn't fit bibliographic data, useful for practitioners feeding data to Europeana, provided it stayed grounded in the schemas' proper definitions (e.g., inscriptions bound to a physical carrier).
key_facts: Michael Hopwood proposed mapping ONIX for Books to LIDO for the Linked Heritage project, including modelling a manifestation/product as if it were a unique item
Patrick Le Boeuf called the mapping impossible in principle because ONIX describes abstractions and LIDO describes unique physical objects, and recommended FRBRoo as the proper target instead
Martin Doerr agreed LIDO was not designed for this and argued interoperability should come from mapping to CRM/FRBRoo-based RDF, not from repurposing LIDO
Regine Stein took a middle position, endorsing the crosswalk as a useful analysis of LIDO's fit and limits without endorsing using LIDO to store this data
produced_answer: In June 2012 (thread 'Bibliographic data in CRM / LIDO - authoritative mappings, help urgently requested'), Michael Hopwood (EDItEUR, Linked Heritage project lead) asked the SIG for help mapping ONIX for Books 3.0.1 to LIDO, for integration of commercial book-industry product data into Europeana. The main objection came from Patrick Le Boeuf (BnF, CRM/FRBR Harmonisation Group), who said he was 'totally perplexed' and that mapping ONIX to LIDO was 'simply impossible': ONIX describes abstract, non-unique publications (better suited to MARC/MODS or FRBRoo), while LIDO is designed for unique physical objects, so treating a 'manifestation' as a unique LIDO item, or printed text as an 'inscription', stretches both models' semantics too far; he also questioned why one would map ONIX to LIDO in the first place. Martin Doerr agreed LIDO was 'not intended for such material' and suggested CRM-FRBRoo would fit better, warning that 'abusing an XML schema for another domain... does not help interoperability,' which should instead come via RDF aggregation under CRM/FRBRoo. Regine Stein (LIDO co-chair) took a more moderating middle position: she distinguished the conceptual models (CRM/FRBRoo) from the XML metadata standards (LIDO/ONIX) and reframed Hopwood's work as a legitimate 'schema crosswalk' / analysis exercise to reveal where LIDO's structures match or fall short of book-industry data needs -- explicitly not implying LIDO should actually be used to encode this data -- and argued such analysis could help identify needed sub-property specializations for interoperability. Hopwood himself defended the exercise (in the companion thread 'Bibliographic data in CRM / LIDO', t0630), noting existing ONIX-MARC mappings already treat many class-level properties as inherited by individual items in practice, that LIDO doesn't explicitly prohibit conceptual objects, and listing several Linked Heritage-driven justifications (EC project mandate, enrichment of heritage/commercial data, linked-data trust via identifiers like ISBN/ISTC/ISNI). The thread was forwarded to the FRBR-CRM Harmonization Group and ended without a resolution -- positions ranged from Le Boeuf's 'impossible, and not clear why one would try' to Doerr's 'not intended, do interoperability via RDF instead' to Stein's 'valid as an analytical crosswalk but not as a data-use recommendation' to Hopwood's practical defense based on project requirements.

question: The SIG discussed how to represent uncertainty about where an archaeological find or activity took place (e.g. 'found near Ankara'). What approaches were proposed for expressing that kind of uncertainty, and which approach did the SIG actually recommend going forward?
gold_answer: The original question proposed reifying the location statement with an E13 Attribute Assignment plus an ad hoc certainty flag. One respondent, drawing on ResearchSpace's practice, argued that E13/P141 lacked precision for annotating a specific statement and described instead using plain RDF reification (rdf:Statement/subject/property/object) combined with the OAC annotation ontology, which had the advantage of letting the object be omitted to talk about a role in general. Martin Doerr explained that P141's range was never defined as 'Property' simply for lack of implementation support at the time, noted that E13/P140/P2/P141 is isomorphic to RDF reification, and said he now regards Named Graphs as a cleaner mechanism than reification for grouping statements together - but stressed that provenance-of-statement machinery like reification or named graphs is a heavy-handed way to express mere certainty/uncertainty. His actual recommendation for uncertainty going forward was not reification or named graphs, but to systematically give CRM properties explicit 'possibly' counterparts (e.g. treating P7_took_place_at as a subproperty of a P7_possibly_took_place_at), guided by a 'recall first' principle so queries still return possibly-correct results instead of nothing under strict open-world semantics.
key_facts: The original proposal was to reify P7_took_place_at via an E13 Attribute Assignment with a custom surety/certainty flag

An alternative described (from ResearchSpace practice) used plain RDF reification (rdf:Statement) combined with the OAC annotation ontology rather than E13, so the object could be omitted to discuss a role generically
Martin Doerr's actual recommendation for uncertainty was to supertype/subtype CRM properties with explicit 'possibly' variants (e.g. a P7_possibly_took_place_at), not reification or named graphs
Martin explicitly distinguished uncertainty/modality from provenance-of-statements, treating reification/named graphs as suited to the latter, not the former
produced_answer: In thread t0610 ("Uncertainty in the location at which an activity took place", March 2012), Alexander Dutton raised the exact 'find location: Ankara(?)' / 'near Ankara' / 'between Mut and Balat' problem and asked how to reify P7_took_place_at with an E13 Attribute Assignment to attach an uncertainty flag. Several approaches were proposed in the discussion: (1) Alexander's original idea of reifying the P7 statement via E13 Attribute Assignment (P140/P141), with an ad-hoc extension property to mark low surety; (2) Vladimir Alexiev's alternative of using RDF Reification vocabulary (rdf:Statement/rdf:subject/rdf:property/rdf:object) or, in ResearchSpace's case, the OAC annotation ontology, to attach a qualification (e.g. 'near', 'between') to the specific statement while still asserting the direct P7 relation; (3) Martin Doerr's counter-proposal that Named Graphs are a cleaner realization of the same E13/RDF-reification isomorphism than plain RDF reification. For the recommendation going forward, Martin (as CRM editor) argued that full reification is 'heavy overkill' for mere certainty/uncertainty modalities, and recommended instead: keep the direct P7_took_place_at assertion (treating all statements as a 'default question mark' so queries still recall results), record the actual uncertainty/qualifier ('near', 'between Mut and Balat', etc.) as a free-text note on the find event rather than in a formal reified structure, and, for encoding discrete uncertainty levels formally, supertype CRM properties with explicit uncertain counterparts (e.g. making P7_took_place_at a subproperty of a new P7_possibly_took_place_at), optionally formalized with modal logic. He proposed this be discussed further at the Helsinki SIG meeting (June 2012), but the archive contains no follow-up thread showing that a formal SIG vote or minutes adopted one option -- the search system's own episode tagging marks this discussion as [unresolved]. So: approaches proposed = E13 attribute-assignment reification, RDF reification/named graphs with statement-level qualifiers, and property supertyping with 'possibly' counterparts; Martin's recommendation (the closest thing to an SIG-level steer in the archive) favored avoiding heavy reification in favor of a note-based qualifier plus the supertyped/modal-logic 'possibly' properties, but this was not shown to be formally ratified by the SIG in the retrieved material.

question: CIDOC CRM has a shortcut property letting a physical object 'depict' something directly, bypassing the conceptual image or inscription it carries. Was a parallel proposal to add equivalent shortcuts for physical objects that merely 'refer to' or are 'about' something (rather than depict it) accepted by the SIG?
gold_answer: No resolution is recorded. A member proposed adding physical-domain siblings of the existing depiction shortcut, so a physical object could state a 'refers to' or 'is about' relationship directly instead of first creating an empty conceptual node just to carry that property. Several members supplied real-world examples meant to establish practice (CRM's usual bar for adding constructs): a gravestone epitaph, a blue plaque referring to both a person and a building, and a museum drawing whose documentation names a play and its scriptwriter. Two members initially argued that in every example the 'aboutness' really belongs to an intermediate conceptual object (such as an inscription) being carried by the physical object, so no new shortcut was needed; the proposer countered that this same argument, if valid, would equally invalidate the existing depiction shortcut, so it could not be used selectively against the new proposal. Martin Doerr laid out CRM's general principle that shortcuts over information-bearing intermediate objects are usually avoided because they can work against information integration, but acknowledged the examples were new evidence CRM-SIG would need to take up at a future meeting. The thread ends with the proposer asking whether the issue had even been logged on the CRM issues list, and no reply on the matter appears in the record - the proposal was left open, neither accepted nor rejected.
key_facts: A member proposed new physical-domain shortcut properties, siblings of the existing 'depicts' shortcut, to avoid creating an empty conceptual node just to carry a 'refers to'/'is about' statement

Two other members argued the 'aboutness' in the examples given (gravestone epitaph, blue plaque, museum drawing referencing a scriptwriter) belongs to an intermediate conceptual object carried by the physical object, not the physical object itself
Martin Doerr said the examples counted as new evidence that CRM-SIG would need to take up at a future meeting, per CRM's practice-based justification principle
The thread ends with no confirmation that the proposal was logged, accepted, or rejected
produced_answer: No. In thread t0630 ("ISSUE: P62 needs a parent and a sibling", July 2012), Vladimir Alexiev proposed adding physical-domain shortcut siblings of P62_depicts — tentatively numbered P67a and P129a — to let a physical object directly 'refer to' (parallel to P67_refers_to) or be 'about' (parallel to P129_is_about) something, mirroring how P62 shortcuts P138_represents. Stephen Stead, Matthew Stiff and Sebastian Rahtz debated examples (blue plaques, gravestone epitaphs, a drawing referencing a scriptwriter), and Martin Doerr gave a detailed theoretical rebuttal arguing that unlike depiction, textual/inscribed 'aboutness' usually passes through an intermediate object (e.g. an inscription) that has its own documentary identity, so shortcutting over it would be counterproductive to information integration; he said CRM-SIG would need to consider the new evidence at a future meeting. No such properties were ever added: the archive's own chronology for P62 tags this episode as 'unresolved', and the current ontology skeleton (v7.1.3) still shows P67 and P129 with only E89 Propositional Object as domain — no E24 Physical Human-Made Thing siblings exist. So the parallel shortcut proposal was discussed but not accepted.

question: When a member wanted to record the language of things like place names and calendar-period names, and asked whether those appellation classes should become subclasses of the Linguistic Object class so the 'has language' property could apply, what did the SIG recommend instead?
gold_answer: The SIG recommended against making appellation classes (place names, time appellations, and similar) into subclasses of E33 Linguistic Object, since most instances of these classes -- most place names, for example -- have no particular language at all, and permanently subclassing them would misrepresent that general case. Martin Doerr's recommended solution was multiple instantiation: a particular appellation that genuinely does have a natural-language form can simply also be declared an instance of E33 Linguistic Object, on a case-by-case basis, alongside its instantiation of the more specific appellation class. Stephen Stead endorsed this, noting that subclassing would effectively be a lie for the many instances where the language-related property doesn't apply, whereas multiple instantiation exists precisely to handle this kind of incidental overlap between classes.
key_facts: The member asked how to apply the 'has language' property to time appellations, place names, and conceptual-object appellations, none of which are subclasses of E33 Linguistic Object.

Martin Doerr recommended multiple instantiation instead of subclassing -- declaring an individual appellation to also be an instance of E33 Linguistic Object when it genuinely has a natural-language form.
Stephen Stead agreed, arguing that making the appellation classes permanent subclasses of E33 would misrepresent the many instances (e.g., most place names) that are not language-specific.
produced_answer: In the September 2014 thread 'More subclasses for E33_Linguistic_Object?', Dan Matei asked how to apply P72 has_language to E49 Time Appellation, E48 Place Name, and E75 Conceptual Object Appellation, and proposed making those classes subclasses of E33 Linguistic Object. Martin Doerr recommended against this: use multiple instantiation instead (e.g. an instance can be declared simultaneously as E49 Time Appellation and E33 Linguistic Object) rather than subclassing. He argued that most appellations (most place names, etc.) do not have a language at all, so making Linguistic Object a superclass of Appellation just because the property sometimes applies would violate the principles of generalization and break the small, clean class hierarchy of the CRM. Stephen Stead agreed explicitly: 'Not all are [linguistic objects], so making them sub-classes is a lie. In those cases where they are, then multiple instantiation is the correct solution.' The episode index confirms this as a 'decided' outcome for the thread.

question: The SIG debated whether coins should be modeled using the FRBRoo class for manifestation product types, treating a coin design the way a book edition is treated. What positions did people take, and what modelling solution did the group actually adopt instead?
gold_answer: Christian-Emil Ore argued coins are information carriers and so belong in the library-oriented FRBRoo hierarchy, comparable to how books are modeled as instances of a Manifestation Product Type. Stephen Stead and Martin Doerr disagreed, arguing a coin's purpose is functional (enabling trade) rather than conveying an 'Expression' the way a text does, with Doerr concluding there was not enough similarity to classify a coin that way. Rather than stretching the FRBRoo manifestation class to cover coins, Maria Theodoridou described extension properties actually built for this purpose: PC1 'produced things of type' (on E12 Production) and PC2 'is example of' (on E22 Man-Made Object), both declared as subproperties of P2 has type, generalizing FRBR's R26 and R7 for categorical/mass production without relying on FRBRoo's information-carrier semantics. Whether the FRBRoo manifestation class itself should eventually be generalized to cover this case was explicitly left open for a future CRM-SIG discussion.
key_facts: Christian-Emil Ore argued coins are information carriers and fit the FRBRoo manifestation-product-type hierarchy used for books; Stephen Stead and Martin Doerr disagreed, saying a coin's purpose is functional/trade-related rather than conveying an Expression.
Martin Doerr concluded there was not enough similarity to classify a coin as a Manifestation Product Type.

Maria Theodoridou described the actual solution adopted for coins: extension properties PC1 'produced things of type' (on E12 Production) and PC2 'is example of' (on E22 Man-Made Object), both subproperties of P2 has type, generalizing FRBR's R26 and R7.
Generalizing the FRBRoo manifestation-product-type class itself to cover coins was left open as a topic for future CRM-SIG discussion, not resolved in this thread.
produced_answer: The debate started when Dan Matei asked whether a coin/coin-issue could be treated as an F3 Manifestation Product Type (with F5 Item R7_is_example_of F3), by analogy to a book edition (thread t0804, 'Coins 2 CRM (again)', Nov 2014). Christian-Emil Smith Ore initially argued yes: coins are information carriers (they carry a design/image) and belong 'in the category of objects found and stored in a library', so FRBRoo's F3 could apply if you care about that aspect. Martin Doerr and Stephen Stead opposed this: Martin argued a coin is acquired for its function as a value token, not to 'get access to the Expression on it' (you don't own 'more Shakespeare' by owning 10 Euro coins), so there is 'not enough similarity to classify a coin as a Manifestation Product Type'; Stephen Stead said a coin's purpose is to enable trade/authenticity, not to carry information, and that F3's scope note would need revising to fit coins. Maria Theodoridou (FORTH) reported that for their own coin project they had NOT reused F3/F5, but instead generalized FRBRoo's R26/R7 into two new CRM-base properties, PC1 'produced things of type' (on E12 Production) and PC2 'is example of' (on E22 Man-Made Object), both declared as subproperties of P2 has type -- explicitly avoiding FRBRoo because 'FRBR is not suitable for our coin modeling since it refers to bibliographic information'. In 2015 homework (threads t0829, t0854, t0856, issues 268/269), Christian-Emil concluded that F3 Manifestation Product Type is inherently publication-specific (its scope note ties it to F24 Publication Expression, hardcover/paperback editions, etc.) and is the wrong place to put coins; he proposed instead modeling mass production in plain, un-extended CIDOC CRM using E12 Production categorized by E55 Type, with the production method captured via E11 Modification. P33 used specific technique: E29 Design or Procedure, and suggested that if this analysis held, CRM should get a new general 'E?? Product Type' class (subclass of E55 Type) rather than stretching F3. This is exactly what the ontology now shows was adopted: CIDOC CRM base contains E99 Product Type (subclass of E55), with properties P186 produced thing of product type (E12 Production -> E99), P187 has production plan (E99 -> E29 Design or Procedure) and P188 requires production tool (E99 -> E19) -- mirroring the E12/E29 model Christian-Emil proposed. E99's own examples explicitly include a coin ('1937 Edward VIII brass threepenny bit') alongside other mass-produced items (a Dragendorff samian vessel, a Qin crossbow part, a Nokia phone, a VW Beetle), while FRBRoo's F3 was left scoped to publications and was later renamed plain 'F3 Manifestation' (in LRMoo); its now-redundant direct link R26 to product type was deprecated in 2022 (thread t1568) once the generic E99-based path took over. So: the group did not extend FRBRoo's manifestation class to cover coins -- it split mass production out into a new CRM-base class, E99 Product Type, used generically for coins and other mass-produced artefacts, leaving F3 Manifestation as a publication-specific class. Note: I could not find the specific proposal/vote thread in which E99 Product Type was formally introduced/accepted -- that step is inferred from the surviving ontology state (concept E99, ontology skeleton) plus the clear trajectory of the 2014-2015 debate, not from a directly retrieved adoption email.

question: When the SIG discussed how to classify a buried hoard of coins, what were the different positions on whether it should be modeled as a curated Collection, and how was the disagreement resolved?
gold_answer: Members disagreed on whether a coin hoard should be an E78 Collection. Christian-Emil Ore suggested it could count as a Collection if a curator had buried their own collection, while Dan Matei worried that ordinary hoard burial does not fit the scope note's requirement of a 'collection development plan.' Stephen Stead argued the underlying problem was the misleading name 'Collection' itself (only half-jokingly proposing renaming the class 'Curated Set'), and Dan separately proposed adding a new intermediate class between Physical Object and Collection to distinguish functional assemblages (like a hoard or suit of armor) from purely physical wholes (like a car). Martin Doerr rejected adding any new class, restating the CRM's minimalism principle that a more specific class should only be introduced when needed to avoid ambiguous or noisy queries; his resolution was that a hoard should simply be treated as an E19 Physical Object typed 'Hoard', reserving E78 Collection (with its curator and curation-plan properties) only for cases where an actual curator and curation activity are documented.
key_facts: Christian-Emil Ore proposed that a hoard qualifies as an E78 Collection only if it was assembled by an actual curator following a collection plan.
Stephen Stead argued the real problem was the class's name 'Collection' and suggested (semi-jokingly) renaming E78 to 'Curated Set'.

Dan Matei proposed a new intermediate class (an 'Assemblage') between E19 Physical Object and E78 Collection to separate functional part-whole relations (hoard, armor) from non-functional ones (car), but Martin Doerr rejected creating it.

Martin Doerr's resolution was that a hoard should default to being modeled as an E19 Physical Object with a type of 'Hoard', with E78 Collection reserved for cases where a documented curator and curation plan exist.
produced_answer: In thread t0809 ('A hoard as crm:E78_Collection?', Nov 29-Dec 1 2014), Dan Matei asked whether a buried coin hoard could be modeled as E78 Collection, worried that the scope note's phrase 'according to a particular collection development plan' didn't fit someone burying coins to retrieve later. Positions varied: Christian-Emil Ore said it could count as a Collection only if a curator-like actor buried it with intent (analogous to a museum curator burying his collection); Simon Spero argued E78's definition was too restrictive, since assembling and curating/preserving roles are conflated in the CRM in a way that doesn't fit archival cases; Stephen Stead said the real problem was the class name 'Collection', which misleads people into thinking the defining trait is the act of collecting rather than curation, and proposed renaming it to something like 'Curated Set'. Martin Doerr took the strongest position: the CRM is not a terminological classification system but a tool for enabling queries, so a hoard should simply be typed as E19 Physical Object with 'type: Hoard' unless you specifically need curator/E87 Curation Activity properties, in which case E78 would be appropriate. He also rejected Dan Matei's proposal for a new intermediate class ('Fx_Assemblage') between E19 and E78, on the grounds that the assemblage/non-assemblage distinction is often undecidable and no concrete querying need had been demonstrated. The thread itself did not reach a clean resolution on the hoard-as-Collection question -- it trailed into a broader methodological debate about when new CRM classes/distinctions are justified, ending with Martin's call for the community to agree on general principles rather than decide this single case. However, Martin's message [6] in the same thread opened a formal issue ('Should we rename E78 Collection?', later Issue 270), and that disagreement was resolved over a year later: in thread t0907 (Feb 2016), the SIG voted and renamed E78 Collection to 'E78 Curated Holding', explicitly to shift the emphasis from 'collecting' to 'curating' (paralleling library usage of 'holdings' for physical copies), which addressed Stephen Stead's naming objection though not by directly re-litigating the hoard example.

question: Did the SIG ever settle the question of whether a CIDOC CRM shortcut property (like a direct 'produced by' link) logically implies the existence of the fuller event-based path it stands in for?
gold_answer: No, the archive shows this was left an open disagreement rather than a settled position. Martin Doerr, working with Carlo Meghini on a first-order-logic formalization of the CRM, argued from a pure-logic standpoint that if a longpath can be inferred, its intermediate nodes logically exist, independent of whether they are ever materialized in a database. Vladimir Alexiev pushed back hard, arguing shortcuts should never entail long-paths in practice: the intermediate node isn't unique, inferring it produces unlocatable 'Skolem' blank nodes that cause problems when integrating richer data later, and by a YAGNI-style principle nothing should be inferred that isn't needed. Christian-Emil Ore and Detlev Balzer largely sided with Doerr's logic-first framing, but the thread ends with Vladimir asking Doerr to clarify his 'soft' versus 'strict' classification of shortcuts, and no reply or resolution appears in the archive.
key_facts: Martin Doerr argued that if a shortcut's underlying longpath can logically be inferred, its intermediate nodes logically exist, treating this as a question of logic separate from database/knowledge-base practice.

Vladimir Alexiev opposed inferring long-paths from shortcuts, citing non-unique intermediates, OWL-inferred blank ('Skolem') nodes that can't be matched during later data integration, and the YAGNI principle.
The thread ends with Vladimir asking Doerr to explain a 'soft' vs. 'strict' classification of shortcuts, and no answer or resolution is recorded.
produced_answer: No universal settlement was ever reached. Martin Doerr opened this as ISSUE: Shortcut semantics in Aug 2014 (thread t0780), arguing that in some cases (e.g. 'created by'/'produced by' standing in for a Production event, or 'rights held by') the shortcut does logically imply the existence of the intermediate event node, while Vladimir Alexiev argued a shortcut should never infer a long path (Skolemization/YAGNI concerns); the thread ended without consensus, and its own episode summary is tagged 'unresolved'. The follow-up homework (Christian-Emil Ore, May 2015, thread t0855) explicitly framed this as informal ('not a formal issue') and concluded the answer varies per property and per person's 'ontological commitment' - some shortcuts were labeled 'strong' (implies the path, e.g. P105 right held by, P56 bears feature) and others 'weak' (does not, e.g. P53/P55 location, P59 has section) - i.e. resolved case-by-case rather than as a general logical rule. The FOL formalization work resurfaced in Oct 2019 (thread t1268) still asking the SIG to 'decide yes or no' property-by-property, with replies like 'we will see' and 'I am unsure here' showing it was still open. Later (2022-2023) the SIG did reach 'decided' status on narrower sub-questions (e.g. defining 'weak inverse' shortcuts, or marking specific CRMbase properties P81/P82 as strong), but never on the general question of whether shortcuts as a class imply their full path.
